new_statements.quote: Stress: We do not usually mark stress in the transliteration, since stress in SH is nearly always penultimate, e.g., ירבה yirbi. In those rare cases in which the transliterated word has ultimate stress, it is marked using the stress mark (ˈ), e.g., זריע zå̄ˈrī. || Corroborating older primary (Petermann 1868: 10-11): "§. 3. Vom Tone. Der Ton ruht, wie im Aramäischen, gegen die Regel der Masorethen, fast stets auf der penultima. Nur in sehr wenigen Fällen bleibt er, wenn das Wort am Ende wächst, auf derselben Silbe, die dann zur antepenultima wird, z. B. מולדת mulédet, מולדתי mulédeti."
new_statements.translation: Petermann: '§ 3. On stress. Stress rests, as in Aramaic and contrary to the rule of the Masoretes, almost always on the penult. Only in very few cases does it remain, when the word grows at the end, on the same syllable, which then becomes the antepenult, e.g. mulédet, mulédeti.'
new_statements.citation: Tal, Abraham & Moshe Florentin. 2025. The Samaritan Pentateuch: An English Translation with a Parallel Annotated Hebrew Text (Cambridge Semitic Languages and Cultures 27). Cambridge: Open Book Publishers, Introduction §4.3.2.8, p. 67.
new_statements.locator: Introduction, §4.3.2.8 'Transliteration Method Used in the Footnotes', p. 67 (PDF p. 84); corroborated by Petermann 1868 § 3 'Vom Tone', pp. 10-11 (PDF pp. 18-19)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (1126 pp., born-digital OBP file, CC BY-NC 4.0, DOI 10.11647/OBP.0415). PDF p. 84 = printed p. 67, Introduction sec. 4.3.2.8 'Transliteration Method Used in the Footnotes'. Text layer and rendered page image both read exactly: "Stress: We do not usually mark stress in the transliteration, since stress in SH is nearly always penultimate, e.g., ירבה yirbi. In those rare cases in which the transliterated word has ultimate stress, it is marked using the stress mark (ˈ), e.g., זריע zåˈrī." (vowel of the last example carries ring + macron). Same page, sec. 4.3.2.9: vowels in closed syllables automatically short, in open syllables long. SH = Samaritan Hebrew per the abbreviation list; GSH =…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in the Samaritan reading tradition of the Pentateuch falls on the penultimate syllable as a near-exceptionless rule (in contrast to the predominantly final stress of Tiberian Hebrew); final stress occurs only in a small, phonologically conditioned residue of words.
new_statements.exceptions: Tal & Florentin: 'rare cases' of ultimate stress, marked with ˈ; their notes (e.g. on assaˈra, diˈdim, baˈrat) explain ultima stress as the result of a dropped guttural or contraction of the last two syllables into one, citing GSH (Ben-Ḥayyim 2000) §1.4.6.1. Hornkohl 2023: 95, citing Ben-Ḥayyim 2000 §§4.4.2–3: ultimate stress is restricted to words with a guttural second or third radical. Petermann 1868: a very few suffixed forms keep stress on the same syllable (antepenult: mulédet ~ mulédeti); a handful of ultima forms (égguj/eggôjem beside elgoj/eggujêm) are errors or exceptions; Petermann attributes the penult stress historically to Aramaic or Arabic influence.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in the liturgical recitation (oral reading tradition) of the Samaritan Pentateuch — SH here = the Samaritan community's reading of the Torah as recorded in Ben-Ḥayyim's LOT IV–V, not a spoken vernacular. Petermann 1868 adds that pausal vowel changes leave no trace. Tal & Florentin also state that vowel length is automatic (long in open, short in closed syllables), so stress is not weight-driven.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog sama1313 'Samaritan' [smp] is Samaritan Hebrew — the Samaritan community's liturgical reading tradition of the Pentateuch (Nablus/Holon) — not Samaritan Aramaic (sama1314; that tradition's penult stress is documented separately in Petermann 1873 under late1255). Tal & Florentin 2025 describe the modern oral reading tradition as recorded in Ben-Ḥayyim's LOT IV–V; Petermann 1868 recorded the pronunciation of Samaritans in Nablus in the 1860s (Genesis transcription). Both are the same tradition; no dialect split.

sources.note: Introduction sec. 4.3.2.8, p. 67 (PDF p. 84, verified on page image): stress in SH is 'nearly always penultimate'; rare ultimate stress is marked with a stress mark in the transliteration. Notes elsewhere attribute ultima stress to a dropped guttural or contraction of the last two syllables, citing GSH (Ben-Hayyim 2000) sec. 1.4.6.1. Same page: vowels in closed syllables automatically short, in open syllables long.

'Stress generally differs from other traditions, being found usually on the penultimate and sometimes on the ultimate.' No citation attached; bibliography lists Ben-Hayyim 2000, Florentin 2005, Rosenberg (Lehrbuch).

sources.note: § 3 'Vom Tone', pp. 10-11 (PDF pp. 18-19, verified on page images): stress rests, as in Aramaic and against the Masoretic rule, almost always on the penult; in very few cases it stays on the same syllable (becoming antepenult) when the word is lengthened at the end (mulédet, mulédeti); a few ultima forms (égguj ~ elgoj) are errors or exceptions; no trace of pausal vowel changes. Also p. 10: vowels kept under inflection 'da bei ihnen der Ton auf der penultima liegt'.
